title: Mitigation of low-frequency underwater anthropogenic noise using stationary encapsulated gas bubbles

# **Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics**

Volume 17, 2012

http://acousticalsociety.org/

## **ECUA 2012 11th European Conference on Underwater Acoustics**

## Edinburgh, Scotland

2 - 6 July 2012

## **Session UW: Underwater Acoustics**

## **UW132.   Mitigation of low-frequency underwater anthropogenic noise using stationary encapsulated gas bubbles**

## **Kevin M. Lee*, Mark S. Wochner and Preston S. Wilson**

## ***Corresponding author’s address: Applied Research Laboratories, The University of Texas at Austin, P.O. Box 8029, Austin, TX 78713-8029, klee@arlut.utexas.edu**

Collections of bubbles cause significant dispersion and attenuation of underwater sound near the individual bubbles’ resonance frequencies and can potentially be used to abate low-frequency anthropogenic underwater noise. Such effects have been reported for large encapsulated bubbles with resonance frequencies below 100 Hz [J. Acoust. Soc. Am. {\bf{127}}:2015 (2010)] and significant attenuation due to bubble resonance phenomena and acoustic impedance mismatching was observed in experiments using a compact electromechanical acoustic source [J. Acoust. Soc. Am. {\bf{128}}:2279 (2010); J. Acoust. Soc. Am. {\bf{129}}:2462 (2011)]. We describe a method of shielding either a noise source or a receiver using screens or curtains of large encapsulated bubbles. This method was applied to two distinct types of real-world noise excitation: continuous wave noise radiated by a vibrating marine vessel and impact noise from marine pile driving. Experimental results show significant noise reduction ranging up to 40 dB can be attained using this method. In addition, a model of encapsulated bubble dynamics was developed and has been used in conjunction with numerical models to design the encapsulated bubble curtain systems. [Work supported by Shell Global Solutions and the ARL:UT IR&D Program.]

Published by the Acoustical Society of America through the American Institute of Physics

## **1 INTRODUCTION**

Many anthropogenic marine activities generate underwater noise louder than the ambient ocean levels in the 10 Hz to 1 kHz frequency range, with much of the acoustic energy being below 500 Hz [1]. Examples of this noise are continuous sources such as radiated noise from ships and their onboard machinery, but can also include impulsive sources such as marine pile driving or explosions [2, 3]. Such noise is a growing concern to industry, regulators, and environmental groups due to its potentially disruptive effects on various species of marine mammals, fish, and aquatic invertebrates [4–6]. Therefore, a means to minimize the acoustic impact of the activities is sought.

The presence of gas bubbles in liquid is known to reduce the speed of sound and greatly increase attenuation relative to bubble-free liquid as well as provide acoustic isolation due to the difference in acoustic impedance between a bubble-free liquid and a bubbly liquid, effects which are proportional to the concentration of bubbles in the liquid [7]. This acoustic impedance mismatch effect has been utilized in an attempt to mitigate underwater anthropogenic noise primarily from pile driving either at the noise source [8] or, more recently, to protect a receiving area [9].

Gas bubbles in water are also known to cause significant dispersion and attenuation of underwater sound near the bubbles’ individual resonance frequency due to absorption and scattering [10–12], a potentially more effective means of noise reduction than acoustic impedance mismatching. A single spherical bubble’s resonance frequency can be estimated using Minnaert’s equation [13]:

where _a_ is the bubble radius, _ν_ is the polytropic exponent for the gas inside the bubble, and _Pl_ and _ρl_ are the hydrostatic pressure and liquid density, respectively. For freely-rising bubbles, such as those used in previous underwater noise mitigation schemes, the spheroidal geometry tends to be unstable for bubble radii greater than approximately 1 cm [14]. Freely-rising bubbles with larger volumes and non-spherical geometries could potentially be used; however, such bubbles tend to become unstable and break up into smaller bubbles [15,16]. Furthermore, currents, waves, and other phenomena in the real-word environment would likely cause additional disruptions to such bubbles. This is unfortunate since a bubble with a resonance frequency near 100 Hz or below would require a radius of several centimeters.

To address this difficulty, large encapsulated bubbles were employed. These large bubbles are created by encapsulating a predetermined volume of air within a thin elastic shell composed of a material such as latex or polyurethane. There are several advantages to using encapsulated bubbles over freely-rising bubbles for noise mitigation purposes. Because the volume of the bubble is deterministic, the resonance frequency can be chosen with a high degree of accuracy, and the resonance frequency can be made as low as needed. Additionally, they may be tethered and used to form a stationary array or curtain in a predetermined position around the noise source. Thus, screens using encapsulated

bubbles are versatile. Previous laboratory studies by the authors showed that large tethered encapsulated bubbles possess the necessary acoustic behavior to be effective as an underwater noise mitigation solution [17].

The main considerations for the shell material surrounding each of these bubbles are that it is thin and elastic enough for the encapsulated air volume to behave acoustically like a bubble, but also that it is rugged enough to survive deployment and usage in a marine environment. A model was developed for describing sound propagation in liquid containing bubbles with solid elastic shells in application to the use of ultrasound contrast agents by Church [18]. In the course of the present work, the authors have also found Church’s model to be useful in predicting resonance frequencies for large encapsulated bubbles as well the dispersion and attenuation of sound as it propagates through collections of such bubbles. The properties of the prospective shell material such as elasticity, density, and thickness can be fine-tuned to optimize the acoustic response of the encapsulated bubble. In general, as the thickness or rigidity of the shell increases for a fixed volume of encapsulated gas, the bubble resonance frequency increases compared to the Minnaert frequency and the amount of attenuation at and above the bubble resonance decreases.

The main objective of this paper is to demonstrate the effectiveness of encapsulated bubbles for mitigating underwater noise in two example cases. First, Church’s analytical model of sound propagation in liquid containing encapsulated bubbles is described, and it is then shown how this model describes results obtained using large tethered arrays of such bubbles reasonably well. This model was used to help design the encapsulated bubble systems discussed in the following sections. A method using a screen of encapsulated bubbles for shielding a noise source consisting of continuous noise radiated by a vibrating work barge is described next. In the second example, a receiving area is shielded from impact noise from pile driving using a curtain of encapsulated bubbles. Finally, it shown how a combination of analytic and numerical modeling is used to design encapsulated bubble arrays, screens, and curtains for other noise sources. The example in this case is a mobile drilling ship.

## **2 SOUND ATTENUATION IN WATER CONTAINING ENCAPSULATED BUBBLES**

In addition to the bubble size and shell material properties, another very important parameter for specifying the level of attenuation or noise reduction provided by an encapsulated bubble array is the ratio of the total volume of gas _V_ g to the total volume of space enclosing the array _V_ tot, or the void fraction _β_ = _V_ g _/V_ tot.

The amount of control over the frequency and level of attenuation provided by a collection of encapsulated bubbles is illustrated using Church’s model [18]. The equations needed to calculate the individual bubble resonance frequency, linear dispersion relation, and damping coefficients are all found in [18]. The attenuation predicted by the equations in [18] for a Gaussian bubble size distribution is plotted in Figure (1) for various void fractions and mean bubble radii. The shell was given the estimated material properties of rubber and had a thickness of 1 mm.

For qualitative comparison with the model predictions, measurements from a set of sound reduction experiments using large tethered encapsulated bubbles with rubber shells were conducted at Lake Travis (a fresh water lake in central Texas, USA). A US-Navy J-13 compact electromechanical acoustic source was suspended from a test barge at a depth of 2.6 m. The frequency of the source was swept between 60 Hz and 2 kHz, and the response was measured on a hydrophone 9.73 m away from the source at a depth of 10 m. Measurements of the response were made with no bubbles in place around the source, then the measurements were repeated with bubble configurations of various bubble sizes and void fractions that matched those used in the calculations. The spectral levels from the various bubble cases were subtracted from the non-bubble case. These quantities were then divided by the distance from the sound source to the edge of the bubble array to estimate the attenuation for the various bubble configurations. The empirical values of attenuation are shown in Figure 1 and are plotted as solid black circles.

Figure 1: _Upper row_ : Comparison of attenuation predicted by the Church model ( _solid grey lines_ ) and measurements from the lake experiment ( _solid circles_ ) for fixed bubble radius of 8 cm and void fractions of 0.005, 0.01, and 0.02, going from left to right. _Lower row_ : Comparison of attenuation predicted by the Church model ( _solid grey lines_ ) and measurements from the lake experiment ( _solid circles_ ) for fixed void fraction of 0.005 and bubble radii of 12 cm, 8 cm, and 6 cm, going from left to right. Note that the scale on vertical axes for each row of plots is different. Also, the frequency is plotted on a log scale for all of the plots.

For the fixed bubble radius case, the bubble resonance frequency predicted by the model is approximately 101 Hz, which agrees well with the frequency of the maximum attenuation in the experimental case. As the void fraction is increased, the amount of attenuation predicted by the model increases. This matching trend is seen in the experimental data. For the fixed void fraction case, the bubble radius was varied from _a_ 0 = 6 cm to _a_ 0 = 12 cm, with predicted resonance frequencies ranging from 175 Hz to 50 Hz. As the encapsulated bubble size is increased, the range of high attenuation shifts to lower frequencies. This trend is also seen in the experimental results as the bubble size is varied.

## **3 SOURCE TREATMENT: A MECHANICALLY VIBRATED BARGE**

A proof-of-concept experiment was conducted in Lake Travis (a fresh water lake in central Texas, USA) using a mechanically-vibrated barge as a noise source. The barge was vibrated by an eccentric motor that was coupled to the barge’s structural components using a four-legged, heavy steel frame. As the barge vibrated, sound was radiated from the hull into the water. The peak frequency of the radiated noise was governed by the rotational speed of the motor and was approximately 70 Hz although harmonics and broadband chaotic noise were also present in the measured spectra. A five-element vertical hydrophone array was deployed at various depths and ranges from the source barge to record the radiated noise. Time domain digital post-processing was performed on the data to extract third-octave band levels. Since the noise source was continuous and the environment was of finite extent, standing wave effects were present and there was significant spatial variation in the acoustic field, hence depth averaging was used. The band levels for data acquired at a particular range and set of experimental conditions were averaged over depth ranging from 2 m to 20 m.

Three basic experimental configurations were applied underneath the vibrating barge: no bubbles; a single-layer screen of 60 encapsulated bubbles, each of which had a resonance frequency of 50 Hz

and were tethered to a weighted frame suspended 0.5 m below the barge; and a screen of small freely-rising bubbles generated by forcing air at a flow rate 0.06 m[3] /s through an array of perforated aeration hoses suspended 2 m below the barge. For the freely-rising bubble case there was a natural distribution of bubbles sizes, but it was estimated using underwater photography that the mean bubble radius was approximately 0.5 cm. It is worth noting that the discrete array of tethered encapsulated bubbles offers a much higher degree of experimental control compared to the air compressor powered freely-rising bubbles. The sound level reduction, shown in Figure 2 measured on a receiver array at a range of 32 m from the source barge, was computed for both versions of the bubble screen by subtracting the band levels for each bubble case from the band levels for the bubble-free case. The encapsulated bubble screen provides as much as 18 dB of reduction near the bubble resonance frequency, and significantly more reduction in general than the freely-rising bubbles at frequencies ranging up to 200 Hz. Furthermore, even though the freely-rising bubbles provide 5 dB–10 dB of reduction at frequencies presumably closer to their resonance frequencies, the encapsulated bubbles seem to perform nearly as well in this frequency range. Some frequencies were not attenuated, but rather enhanced in the presence of the bubbles. Such behavior tended to occur well below bubble resonance, and this effect was more pronounced in the case of the freely-rising bubbles.

Figure 2: Sound level reduction computed in one-third octave frequency bands for treating the mechanically-vibrated barge source with either encapsulated bubbles ( _black_ ) and freely-rising bubbles ( _grey_ ).

## **4 RECEIVER TREATMENT: SHIELDING FROM PILE DRIVING NOISE**

A water treatment plant construction project in Lake Travis was used as a source-of-opportunity in an experiment where a distant receiving area was shielded from incoming impulse sounds generated by the pile driving events. The pile driving was approximately 2.5 km from the receiving area. The piles being driven were composed of 1.2-m-diameter steel pipe. The average measured peak-topeak sound pressure level generated by the pile driving events was 185 dB re 1 _μ_ Pa at a distance of 112 m from the pile. The average sound pressure level at the receiving area 2.5 km away was 150 dB re 1 _μ_ Pa, prior to treatment by the bubble screen. The peak pressures were observed in the 100 Hz–300 Hz frequency range. The data was acquired over multiple hammer strikes on eight different piles.

For the purposes of the experiment, the receiving area consisted of the area under the test barge, previously mentioned in Section 2. A schematic of the encapsulated bubble curtain and test apparatus is shown in Figure 3. The curtain consisted of twenty-four 20-m-long lines each spaced at a horizontal distance of 1.25 m. Each line contained encapsulated bubbles separated by a vertical distance of 27 cm for a total of nearly nine hundred bubbles in the curtain. The bubble size was chosen

such that the resonance frequency was approximately 100 Hz at mid-depth. In reality there was a distribution of bubble sizes due to hydrostatic pressure. Note that the curtain only partially protected the receiving area, as seen in Figure 3, so some of the reflections due multipathing in the lake were able to penetrate the receiving area without passing through the curtain. The impulses from the pile driving events were measured simultaneously on the horizontal array of three receivers shown in the schematic. One of the receivers R1 was located in front of the curtain while two receivers R2 and R3 were located behind the curtain. All three receivers were deployed at the same depth, which was varied from 2 m to 20 m over various pile driving events. The purpose of varying the depth of the receiver array was measure the impulses at various points within the waveguide on both sides of the curtain so that spatially-dependent effects could later be minimized with averaging.

Post-processing of the raw data was performed as follows. Power spectral densities were computed from the individual impulse waveforms, then the spectra were put into 30 Hz frequency bands with levels expressed in dB re 1 _μ_ Pa. The differences between the band-limited spectra between R1 and R2 as well as R1 and R3 were used to compute the power spectral density reduction in dB for each pile driving event. These values were then averaged over many pile driving events for each receiver pair, which by nature of the data acquisition were measured at various depths within the waveguide. Finally, the results for both receiver pairs were averaged together. The resultant mean power spectral density reduction due to the presence of the encapsulated bubble curtain is plotted in Figure 3. The amount of averaging applied to the data was performed due to the variability of sound source over the course of the experiment, which included variability of the signal not only from pile to pile, but also from strike to strike. Even with the receiving area only being partially shielded from pile driving noise, the curtain still provides up to 14 dB of level reduction in the peak energy frequency range of 100 Hz–300 Hz, indicating that such a treatment could work well for sensitive marine areas that may need protection from marine construction noise.

Figure 3: _Left_ : Measurement layout for pile driving experiment. _Right_ : Average power spectral density reduction for pile driving impulses transmitted through the curtain between the R1-R2 and R1-R3 receiver pairs.

## **5 MODELING AND DESIGN OF DEPLOYMENT SYSTEMS**

A combination of the appropriate effective medium analytical model and finite-element numerical modeling is used in the design of noise mitigation systems for real-world applications. An example of this is a bubble curtain designed to abate radiated noise from a moored drilling ship. The geometry of the system is shown in Figure 4. The domain was a fully three-dimensional cylindrical geometry that consisted of a water medium with a pressure release boundary condition on top, a rigid boundary condition on bottom, and a radiation boundary condition at the edges, which assumed cylindrical spreading. The diameter of the domain was 200 m and the height or depth was 30 m. The sound source, which was centered in the domain and was placed near the surface, had a geometry based

on a mobile cylindrically-symmetric ice-breaking drilling ship named the Kulluk [4]. The diameter of the sound source was 70 m and the maximum depth of the sound source was nearly 10 m. A normal acceleration condition of 1 m/s[2] was applied to all surfaces of the source geometry to simulate vibration of the ship’s hull caused by onboard machinery. The simulation was performed in the frequency domain at a frequency of 50 Hz, and the steady-state solution was computed at all points in space. The model was then run with various bubble curtain configurations to determine the most effective curtain design.

Figure 4: _Left_ : Simulation and encapsulated bubble curtain geometry used. _Right_ : Sound pressure level as a function of range at a depth of 15 m and fixed azimuthal angle for three cases: no vertical curtain lines ( _solid black_ ), 39 vertical curtain lines ( _solid grey_ ), and 156 vertical curtain lines ( _dashed grey_ ) Each line consists of an effective medium with 50 Hz bubbles and a void fraction of 2%.

The curtain shown in Figure 4 consisted of a spiral set of vertical lines at an average stand-off distance of 15 m from the outer edge of the drilling ship’s hull. The spiral shape was chosen so that the curtain could have an opening in which the two ends have some amount of overlap. The functional purpose of the opening was to allow for tender ships to pass through and service the moored drilling ship. Additionally, the curtain rises up only 27 m from the bottom boundary, leaving a 3 m gap between the top of the curtain and the water surface to allow smaller support vessels to traverse the curtain.

Instead of modeling the vertical curtain lines with discrete bubbles, an effective medium approach was used. Each individual line was modeled as a bubbly liquid cylinder with a length of 27 m and a diameter equal to one bubble diameter. The bubble size was chosen to have a resonance frequency of 50 Hz, and the void fraction was chosen so that the density of bubbles in each cylinder was equivalent to having a vertical bubble spacing of approximately one bubble diameter, which corresponds to a void fraction of approximately 33% for each cylinder. Keeping the void fraction in each cylinder fixed, the number of vertical lines in the curtain, and hence the line spacing, was varied and the model was re-iterated for each case.

The sound pressure level at depth of 15 m and fixed azimuthal angle for a source frequency of 50 Hz is plotted as a function of range for three curtain scenarios in Figure 4. The drilling ship is centered at the origin and extends to a range of 30.48 m, as shown by the left-most vertical dotted line. The location of the curtain in this one-dimensional slice of the acoustic field is 45.48 m, shown by the other vertical dotted line. For the case with no curtain, the propagation is governed solely by the geometry of the waveguide. For the case with 39 vertical lines, the pressure is somewhat increased inside of the curtain; however, it drops by approximately 5 dB outside of the curtain. For the case with 156 vertical lines, the pressure is decreased by 30 dB outside of the curtain, indicating a highly effective curtain design. The corresponding global void fractions, that is the void fraction for the entire curtain, for the 39 line and 156 line cases are 0.9% and 3.5% respectively, indicating that very little air is used throughout the overall volume of the curtain to achieve these results.

## **6 SUMMARY**

Large air cavities with elastic shells resonate acoustically like bubbles as long as the shell material is not too thick or too rigid. Sound propagation in water through collections of such large encapsulated bubbles is described reasonably well by Church’s effective medium model. This was illustrated qualitatively by a comparison between the model predictions and experimental results using an array of tethered air-filled rubber shells. A more rigorous comparison would require more precise knowledge of the shell’s material properties, and such a comparison between experiment and Church’s model, as well as other versions of the model, is the subject of current ongoing research by the authors.

Encapsulated bubble screens were applied in the mitigation of noise in two real-world systems. A screen of encapsulated bubbles reduced radiated noise from a mechanically-vibrated barge with an observed peak band level reduction of up to 18 dB near the bubble resonance frequency. The bubble size was chosen so that the screen provided the most attenuation at frequencies near the peak frequencies emitted by the noise source. In the second example, an encapsulated bubble curtain was used to partially shield a receiving area from underwater pile driving noise, and the curtain provided more than 10 dB of noise reduction in the 100 Hz–300 Hz frequency band coincident with the peak frequencies generated by the pile driving events.

Next, it was shown how a combination of the effective medium model approach describing the bubble dynamics and a numerical modeling approach describing the noise source, the bubble treatment geometry, and the propagation in a shallow waveguide environment can be used to aid in the design of a large-scale encapsulated bubble noise mitigation system. The example given was an encapsulated bubble curtain for mitigating radiated noise from the hull of a stationary drilling ship. The design also incorporated practical aspects, such as including an opening for support vessels to tend to the drilling ship.

As a few final comments, it is worthwhile to point out some of the practical advantages concerning the use of tethered encapsulated bubbles as opposed to freely-rising bubbles or other previously used noise mitigation treatments. Once an encapsulated bubble screen or curtain is deployed, there is no need to further expend energy to maintain its functionality. This is not the case for freelyrising bubbles, which require a continuous supply of air. This air is often provided by industrial air compressors, which require fuel to operate, making them not only expensive to run, but also burn fossil fuels and create their own airborne noise. The encapsulated bubble system would be deployed before the noise generating activity takes place, and would only need to be recovered when the activity is completed. An array of tethered encapsulated bubbles does require ballast to hold it down, but this can easily be designed into the system and readily dealt with during the deployment and recovery. In terms of treating a drilling ship as in the modeling example, the use of freely-rising bubbles would impractical due to the vast amount of air supply needed to generate such a large curtain. De-watered cofferdams are sometimes used for mitigating pile driving noise, but these systems would be far more expensive and difficult to deploy than an encapsulated bubble system. Thus, in addition to the effectiveness and tailorability of encapsulated bubble based systems, many practical reasons make them a very desirable noise mitigation solution.
